title: Ἀλέκτορες δύο καὶ ἀετός
titleEn: The Two Cocks and the Eagle
part: The Two Cocks and the Eagle (Chambry 20)
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 20. Text as printed, including Chambry's editorial punctuation (« », ⟨ ⟩ for editorial supplements). Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Ἀλεκτόρων δύο μαχομένων περὶ θηλειῶν ὀρνίθων, ὁ εἷς τὸν ἕτερον κατετροπώσατο.
sentences.tr: Alektorōn dyo machomenōn peri thēleiōn ornithōn, ho heis ton heteron katetropōsato.
sentences.l: Two cocks fighting over the hen birds, the one routed the other.
sentences.i: Two cocks were fighting over the hens, and one of them routed the other.
sentences.n: A genitive absolute again, the standard Aesopic way of opening a scene. θήλειαι ὄρνιθες, “female birds”, is simply the hens. κατατροπόομαι, “put to rout”, is a word from the battlefield; the fable keeps military vocabulary for a barnyard quarrel throughout.

sentences.t: Καὶ ὁ μὲν ἡττηθεὶς εἰς τόπον κατάσκιον ἀπιὼν ἐκρύβη· ὁ δὲ νικήσας εἰς ὕψος ἀρθεὶς καὶ ἐφ’ ὑψηλοῦ τοίχου στὰς μεγαλοφώνως ἐβόησε.
sentences.tr: Kai ho men hēttētheis eis topon kataskion apiōn ekrybē· ho de nikēsas eis hypsos artheis kai eph’ hypsēlou toichou stas megalophōnōs eboēse.
sentences.l: And the one who had been beaten, going off into a shadowy place, hid himself; but the one who had won, having been lifted up on high and having stood on a lofty wall, crowed at the top of his voice.
sentences.i: The beaten cock went off into a shady corner and hid; the winner rose into the air, took his stand on a high wall and crowed at the top of his voice.
sentences.n: ὁ μέν… ὁ δέ… is “the one… the other…”: with the article alone Greek needs no nouns at all. ἐκρύβη is an aorist passive doing middle duty, “hid himself”. The two halves are built alike: an aorist participle for the outcome of the fight (ἡττηθείς, νικήσας), more participles for what followed (ἀπιών present, “going off”; ἀρθείς and στάς aorist), and one main verb at the end of each — the ordinary shape of narrative here, and the reason the crow lands so hard.

sentences.t: Καὶ παρευθὺς ἀετὸς καταπτὰς ἥρπασεν αὐτόν.
sentences.tr: Kai pareuthys aetos kataptas hērpasen auton.
sentences.l: And straightway an eagle, having swooped down, snatched him up.
sentences.n: καταπτάς is the aorist participle of καταπέτομαι, “fly down”. The eagle is Zeus's own bird, which sharpens the point: the crowing from the top of the wall is answered from higher up still.

sentences.t: Ὁ δ’ ἐν σκότῳ κεκρυμμένος ἀδεῶς ἔκτοτε ταῖς θηλείαις ἐπέβαινε.
sentences.tr: Ho d’ en skotōi kekrymmenos adeōs ektote tais thēleiais epebaine.
sentences.l: And the one hidden in darkness thereafter mounted the hens without fear.
sentences.n: κεκρυμμένος is a perfect participle: not “having hidden” but “in a state of concealment”, still hidden. ἐπιβαίνω with the dative is the plain animal-breeding word, and the fable does not soften it. The imperfect ἐπέβαινε makes it a settled state of affairs, not one occasion.

sentences.t: Ὁ μῦθος δηλοῖ ὅτι Κύριος ὑπερηφάνοις ἀντιτάσσεται, ταπεινοῖς δὲ δίδωσι χάριν.
sentences.tr: Ho mythos dēloi hoti Kyrios hyperēphanois antitassetai, tapeinois de didōsi charin.
sentences.l: The fable shows that the Lord ranges himself against the arrogant, but to the lowly gives favour.
sentences.n: This moral is not pagan: it is Proverbs 3:34 in its Septuagint wording, the verse the New Testament quotes at James 4:6 and 1 Peter 5:5 (with “God” for “the Lord”). Almost certainly a Christian-era hand has put it here in place of whatever moral once closed the fable, though nothing in the text says so; Chambry prints it without brackets. Κύριος without the article is the Septuagint's standing rendering of the divine name. ἀντιτάσσομαι is “draw up against” in the line of battle, keeping the military vocabulary the fable began with; χάρις here is favour, goodwill shown from above.
